newsitem.title: POLAND: TURKISH OFFICIAL CALMS POLAND'S NATO WORRIES.
newsitem.headline: TURKISH OFFICIAL CALMS POLAND'S NATO WORRIES.

text.p: A senior Turkish official on Monday assured Poland that Ankara was unlikely to carry out a threat to obstruct its path to NATO as a means to advance Turkey's case for European Union entry.

Ankara in January aroused concern in Warsaw, which sees fast NATO entry as a key goal, by threatening to block the Western military alliance's eastward enlargement unless Turkey was granted full EU membership.

After talks with Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski in Warsaw on Monday, Turkey's Undersecretary for Foreign Affairs Onur Oymen told reporters that his country supported NATO's enlargement and wished only to be treated fairly in its own EU bid.
"Provided that fairness prevails, there will be no problem in the enlargement of any European organisation," he said.

Asked whether Turkey would block NATO expansion, Oymen said: "We are promised by practically all governments of Europe that Turkey will be treated fairly. Therefore we do not need to stress the negative side of the coin."

In a reference to early March statements by some centrist European Union leaders who said Turkey did not qualify partly because it was an Islamic state, Oymen said EU doors should not be closed to anyone for religious or cultural reasons.
He said EU foreign ministers had accepted this principle at a meeting in the Netherlands on March 16 and Turkey expected their views to be treated as the Union's official position.
Warsaw, which escaped Moscow's domination after the 1989 collapse of communism, expects to be invited to begin talks on joining NATO at the alliance's Madrid summit in July.
It needs the consent of each member state's parliament, including Turkey's, before it can join as planned in 1999.
Oymen has been in Poland over the weekend for a meeting of a special senior consultative committee set up between the two countries by former Polish President Lech Walesa.

The committee discussed details of a planned visit in May by Turkey's President Suleyman Demirel, who will be accompanied by a large group of business representatives, and prospects for an agreement freeing trade between the two countries.
A Kwasniewski aide said the committee had spoken of prospects for Polish involvement in the power-generating industry in Turkey and for Turkish firms to engage in the building of Polish motorways.
